h1:
Isan Food in Kalasin
Som Tam, Laab, Koi & Grilled Chicken Locals Actually Eat
intro: Kalasin is a town that takes its laab and koi seriously. People here meet up at roadside laab-koi spots just as often as at the som tam stalls in the market. Most of the good places aren't fancy — they're the kind of spot locals keep coming back to until it becomes their regular, and a few have been open for over 30 years. We pulled this list together from local reviews, with the neighborhood, rough prices and the dishes worth ordering at each one.

blocks.html: Isan food in Kalasin is all about laab and koi, with that savory depth that comes from proper Isan-style fermented fish (pla daek). The town has legendary laab-koi joints passed down through several generations, alongside roadside som tam stalls and long-running market spots. Prices are still easy on the wallet — som tam runs 40–70 THB a plate, laab and koi start around 60 THB. We gathered the places that come up most often in local reviews and tell you straight what each one does best. We haven't eaten at every spot ourselves; this is pieced together from real reviews we could find.

blocks.text: Ranking the Isan restaurants Kalasin locals actually go to

blocks.html: This ranking is ordered by how often a place comes up in reviews and how popular it is with locals — it doesn't mean the ones lower down are any less tasty. Each spot stands out for something different, so pick based on the dish you're craving and the neighborhood that's convenient for you. The prices listed are rough per-plate estimates and can shift with the season and ingredients. Double-check opening hours before you go, since some places adjust their times depending on the season.

items.name: Look Chai Kamnan Boonsong
items.blurb: Kalasin's legendary laab-koi joint, handed down from father to son over nearly 30 years — it's the first name that comes to mind when locals talk about laab and koi. It nails the laab, dry koi (koi pong), lime koi and the spicy hotpot tom saap that nearly every table orders. There's grilled fish, grilled chicken and roast duck to go with it. Bold, savory and properly herby in true Isan style, it's great for a group.
items.meta: Bypass Road, Mueang district (branch in Yang Talat) · open roughly 8:00–22:00 daily

items.name: Laem Thaen Laab Koi
items.blurb: A well-known Isan restaurant across the province, with its big branch on the Yang Talat side along Thinanon Road. It's known for carefully seasoned laab and koi — balanced but still punchy — and you can order som tam, tom saap and grilled dishes all in one place. Comfortable seating for groups, and a spot that people from Yang Talat and town drive over to regularly.
items.meta: Thinanon Rd, Yang Talat district · open roughly 9:00–21:00 daily

items.name: Pu Laab Ped Thee Det Kalasin
items.blurb: A duck laab spot that Kalasin locals review a lot. The look is more relaxed than your typical laab joint but the flavors are still proper Isan. The stars are the duck laab and soi ju, which plenty of people come specifically to order. There's grilled pork neck, sweet liver and fresh prawn yum to pair it with — good for anyone who wants duck laab in a laid-back evening setting.
items.meta: Mueang Kalasin city area · mainly dinner

items.name: Tam Yua Yeah (Your Yeah)
items.blurb: A standout som tam spot in town that the younger crowd loves. It's known for over-the-top plates like the seafood-loaded tam yua yeah, crispy noodle tam with cockles, and crispy noodle tam with moo yo. There's tom, yum and grilled dishes to go with it, all seasoned with a heavy, herby hand — great if you like a loud, loaded plate and want to try several styles of tam in one sitting.

items.name: Taeng Som Tam
items.blurb: An in-town som tam spot on Thanapol Road that Kalasin locals stop by regularly. The menu covers it all — som tam, grilled chicken, nam tok and laab — with a savory hand and friendly prices. It's the classic som tam–grilled chicken–sticky rice combo from a familiar regular, easy to order and easy to eat. Good for lunch or dinner without having to dig down some back alley.
items.meta: Thanapol Rd, Mueang district · open 10:00–21:00 daily

items.name: Huean Kalasin–Suan Don Tham
items.blurb: An open-air garden restaurant in the Ban Sa-at Tai area of Nuea subdistrict, ranked among the province's popular Isan spots in reviews. It's built for long, lingering meals with family or a big group, with som tam, pork laab and Isan dishes to pair with regional menus. Open late, it's good for a dinner when you want comfortable seating.
items.meta: Ban Sa-at Tai, Nuea subdistrict, Mueang district · open 10:00–23:00 daily

items.name: To Koi Kalasin
items.blurb: A laab-koi spot that reviewers praise for its beef laab and well-seasoned koi. You can choose beef or pork laab, with fragrant roasted rice powder and fresh meat. It's a small laab-koi joint in true Isan style that beef-laab fans keep coming back to — good for anyone who wants bold laab at a low price.

items.name: Laab Kalasin Shop, JPR School Fresh Market
items.blurb: A laab spot in the JPR School fresh market area that locals treat as a go-to. It's a community shop that's been selling laab, koi and Isan dishes for years — cheap, fresh and quick. Good for a lunchtime stop or takeaway, and more of a neighborhood regular than a social-media darling.
items.meta: JPR School fresh market area, Mueang district · lunch

items.name: Ping Kai Yai Duean
items.blurb: An old-school grilled chicken spot that Kalasin locals call a town legend. It's been selling so long it's become the regular for people in the area — fragrant, well-marinated chicken with skin grilled just right, perfect with som tam and sticky rice. The chicken sells out fast in the evening, so go before dusk if you want some. Great for anyone hunting down the town's old-guard grilled chicken.
items.meta: Mueang Kalasin city area · lunch–dinner (chicken sells out fast)

items.name: Saap Kalasin
items.blurb: A som tam spot that started as a pushcart before opening as a shop. Reviewers say the seasoning is punchy and worth the price, with a wide range of tam, grilled chicken and laab to go with it. It's an in-town som tam spot with friendly prices — good if you want bold, homestyle tam without going to a big restaurant, and a full meal that won't dent the budget.

items.name: Suan Ahan Kalasin Kung Phao
items.blurb: A comfortable garden restaurant known for its grilled prawns (kung phao), but with a full lineup of som tam and Isan food to go alongside. Good if you want big grilled prawns with bold tam and laab in one meal. The setting is open and easy for a group, and it stays open late — great for an evening get-together when you want both grilled stuff and something spicy.
items.meta: Mueang Kalasin city area · open 10:00–22:00 daily
items.price: Som tam–laab ฿50–90 · grilled prawns by weight

blocks.title: An honest note about koi
blocks.html: A lot of koi in Kalasin is still served raw or partly cooked, especially raw freshwater-fish koi, which carries a risk of liver fluke that's common in the Isan region. If you're not used to raw dishes, order cooked koi or cooked laab instead — just tell the shop you want it cooked and most places can do it.

blocks.text: Dishes to order at an Isan restaurant in Kalasin

items: Laab–koi — the town's headliner. Pork or beef laab dusted with fragrant roasted rice powder; for koi, order it cooked if you're not used to raw dishes.
Tom saap hotpot — a hot, punchy soup that nearly every table orders at the famous laab-koi joints; it cuts through the richness of the laab nicely.
Duck laab–soi ju — the town's signature spicy plates, found at many spots. Duck laab is firm and meaty, while soi ju is eaten with a jaew dipping sauce.
Som tam pla ra — the foundational tam, savory from local fermented fish. Tell the shop your spice level when you order.
Grilled chicken — fragrant, well-marinated chicken eaten with sticky rice and jaew; at the famous spots the chicken sells out fast in the evening.

blocks.text: Which neighborhoods are easiest for Isan food

blocks.html: In town, Kalasin's tam and laab-koi spots are spread out everywhere, especially along the Bypass Road, which has the famous laab-koi joints. The Thanapol Road area and around the JPR School fresh market are where locals eat, and if you prefer a long, lingering garden meal there's the Nuea subdistrict zone and the city outskirts that suit a group. If you're driving in from Yang Talat, there are roadside laab-koi spots along Thinanon Road to stop at on the way. Most places aren't far apart and are easy to reach by car.

items.name: Bypass Road zone
items.blurb: Famous laab-koi joints with comfortable seating and easy parking — good for an evening with a group.

items.name: Market zone (Thanapol–JPR School)
items.blurb: In-town tam, laab and grilled chicken at friendly prices — where locals genuinely eat.

items.name: Garden restaurants on the outskirts
items.blurb: Roomy group spots in the Nuea subdistrict zone and outskirts, strong on grilled prawns and fish dishes.

blocks.title: If you're stopping to eat on a dinosaur-trail trip
blocks.html: A lot of people come to Kalasin for the Sirindhorn Museum and the dinosaur footprints around Sahatsakhan. If that's your plan, eat your Isan meal in town as a stop before or after heading up, since most of the famous spots are in the city area. And on the way to the Lam Pao Dam there are roadside som tam stalls to refuel at.

blocks.text: How to eat Isan in Kalasin like a local and get your money's worth

items: Hit the grilled chicken spots before dusk — at the famous ones the chicken sells out fast, often from around 5pm onward.
Carry cash. Some som tam stalls in the market and along the road still take cash only, though many places now have PromptPay.
State your spice level when you order. The standard heat here is noticeably hotter than in central Thailand.
Order extra sticky rice — laab, tam and grilled chicken all need sticky rice to feel right.
If you're not used to raw dishes, skip raw fish koi and go for cooked koi or cooked laab to be safer.

faq.q: Which Isan restaurants in Kalasin do locals actually go to?
faq.a: The most talked-about spots are Look Chai Kamnan Boonsong, the legendary laab-koi joint on Bypass Road that's been open nearly 30 years, Laem Thaen Laab Koi on the Yang Talat side, Pu Laab Ped Thee Det Kalasin, and in-town som tam spots like Tam Yua Yeah (Your Yeah) and Taeng Som Tam on Thanapol Road. All of them are places locals come back to, at prices that are easy on the wallet.

faq.q: Roughly how much does som tam, laab and koi cost in Kalasin?
faq.a: Som tam runs about 40–70 THB a plate, laab and koi around 50–100 THB depending on the ingredients, and duck laab and soi ju around 80–150 THB. The tom saap hotpot at the famous laab-koi spots starts around 120 THB and up, and grilled chicken starts around 60 THB a bird. It's good value when you eat as a group.

faq.q: Is it safe to eat koi in Kalasin?
faq.a: Some koi is still served raw or partly cooked, especially raw freshwater-fish koi, which carries a risk of liver fluke that's common in the Isan region. If you're not used to raw dishes, order cooked koi or cooked laab instead — just tell the shop you want it cooked and most can do it.

faq.q: Where should I go for Kalasin's famous laab and koi?
faq.a: Look Chai Kamnan Boonsong on Bypass Road is the legendary laab-koi joint locals think of first, known for its laab, lime koi and tom saap hotpot. Laem Thaen Laab Koi on the Yang Talat side is another spot reviewers rave about. If you like duck laab, try Pu Laab Ped Thee Det Kalasin.

faq.q: Do Isan restaurants in Kalasin accept transfers?
faq.a: Most in-town and larger restaurants have PromptPay, but some small som tam stalls in the market or along the road still take cash only. It's best to carry some cash just in case.
